transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, thank you for seeing me. I, um, I’m really struggling right now, and it’s honestly taking over my life. I’m here because I just can’t stop seeing this... this terrible droop and unevenness around my mouth and my jaw. It’s like the left side is just sagging down completely differently than the right, and the skin looks so heavy and distorted. Every single time I see a photo of myself, or if I catch a glimpse in a window or a mirror—which I try not to do, but it’s impossible to avoid them completely—it’s just right there, staring back at me. It’s so jarring. 

And the thing is, my husband, my friends, they all tell me I look fine, that they don't see what I'm talking about, or that it's just normal aging. But they have to be lying to make me feel better, or they just aren't looking closely enough, because to me, it is glaringly obvious. It’s so noticeable that I’ve actually started avoiding giving presentations at work. I’m an architect, so presenting to clients is a huge part of my job, but I just can't stand the thought of them staring at my face, judging how lopsided and awful it looks while I'm trying to explain a design. I’ve even started passing off some of my best clients to my colleagues just so I don't have to sit in a room with them. I just... I don't know how to stop obsessing over it, and it's ruining my career.
Is it only your mouth and jaw that you're concerned about, or are there other parts of your body that you also worry about?

No, no, it’s really just… I mean, I know a lot of women my age, they complain about their weight or their hips, or, you know, getting wrinkles around their eyes, but I honestly couldn't care less about any of that. It is entirely, one hundred percent just this… this lower part of my face. My mouth and my jaw. 

If my arms are a little flabby, I can just put on a cardigan or a nice tailored blazer, you know? I have a whole closet of beautiful, professional clothes for work. But you can’t put a blazer over your face. Your face is your identity, it’s what people look at when you speak to them, and when I speak, I just know they are watching that left side droop and wobble. 

I don't even have the mental energy to think about the rest of my body because this one specific area just consumes everything. It’s like a black hole. I will literally stand in the bathroom for hours, just… just pressing my fingers against my cheek, pulling the skin back up and back toward my ear to where it’s supposed to be, trying to see what I looked like before it all just collapsed on that side. And I think, if I could just fix this one terrible, glaring asymmetry, just this one thing, my life would go back to normal and I could actually look my clients in the eye again. So, no, I don't worry about my nose or my stomach or anything else. Just the jaw. Just the way the corner of my mouth pulls down so heavily… it’s just ruined my entire face.
Do you ever think that maybe your husband and friends are telling the truth and your jaw actually looks normal?

I... I mean, I try to. I really, really try to believe them. Sometimes, for a split second, I’ll think, "Okay, maybe my husband is right, maybe he sees me every day and he would know if something was really that horribly wrong." He’s a good man, you know? We’ve been married for twenty-five years, and he’s always been so supportive. So I tell myself, maybe he’s telling the truth. But then... then I walk past the hall mirror, or I catch my reflection in the microwave door when I'm making my morning coffee, and it just shatters that tiny bit of hope completely. 

Because I can see it. It’s not a feeling, it’s not something I’m imagining—it is physically right there. The skin on the left side, right at the jowl, it just hangs lower. The shadow it casts in overhead lighting is completely different from the right side. And when I point that out to my friends, when I say, "Look, look at this shadow right here, look at how the corner of my lip turns down on the left but not the right," they just give me this... this pitying look. They say, "Oh, honey, we all get older, nobody is perfectly symmetrical." But it’s not just normal aging! It’s not just a little wrinkle! It’s a complete structural collapse on one side of my face! 

So, no, I just... I can't believe them. I think they love me and they don't want me to be in pain, so they minimize it. Or maybe they’re just so used to my face that they don't look at it critically anymore. But strangers do. Clients do. When I’m standing at the head of a conference table under those awful fluorescent office lights, pointing at a blueprint, I know they aren't looking at the design. I know they are staring at my jawline and wondering what happened to me. So how can I believe my friends when the evidence is literally right there on my face every single time I look? I just... I can't. I know what I see.
Do you think it's possible that your perception of your jawline is not entirely accurate?

I... I don't know how that could be possible. I mean, how can my perception be wrong when it's right there in front of me? That's exactly why I'm sitting here in this chair today. I’m here because I just can’t stop seeing this droop and this awful unevenness around my mouth and my jaw. It's not just a feeling in my head. It's in every single photograph someone takes of me. It's in every reflection, every mirror, every dark window I walk past at night. 

And I know, I know I've said that my husband and my friends tell me I look fine, and maybe they really do mean it, but... but it feels so undeniably obvious to me. It's not like I'm looking at a blurry picture and guessing; I see the sagging skin, I see the way the left side is just completely heavier than the right. It's so glaringly obvious that it's literally changing how I live my life. I mean, I’m an architect! I’m supposed to be confident. But I’ve started avoiding giving presentations entirely. I’m dodging my clients, passing off projects I worked for months to secure, all because I cannot stand the thought of them looking at my face and seeing what I see. 

So when you ask if my perception is inaccurate... how can it be? If it were just in my head, why would it look the exact same in a photograph as it does in the mirror? Why would the shadow fall exactly where the droop is? I just... I don't understand how it could be my perception when the physical proof is right there every time I look. It’s all I can see.
Have you ever considered the possibility that the flaw you see in your jawline is not noticeable to others because it doesn't actually exist?

Doesn't actually exist? Doctor, I... I feel like we are just going in circles here. Like I was just trying to explain to you a moment ago, I am sitting in this office, talking to a professional, specifically because I absolutely cannot stop seeing this. It is all I see. Every single time I look in a mirror, every time I catch my reflection in the glass doors of my firm's lobby, every single photograph someone takes... it is right there. This awful, heavy droop and the unevenness around my mouth and my jaw. 

You ask me to consider that it doesn't exist, and I know people tell me I look fine—my husband, my friends, they all say these things to placate me—but it feels so incredibly, undeniably obvious to me. It's not a ghost. It's not some imaginary concept. If it didn't exist, why would it be dictating my entire life? 

I mean, like I said, I'm an architect. I've spent decades building my reputation from the ground up. I thrive on pitching designs. And now? Now I am actively avoiding my own clients. Just last Thursday, we had a major pitch for a commercial complex downtown—a project I spearheaded, I drew the primary elevations myself—and I faked a migraine so my junior partner could do the presentation. I literally sat in my car in the parking garage and cried for an hour because I couldn't bear the thought of standing at the front of that boardroom where everyone would see the left side of my jaw sagging. I am throwing away my career! I'm avoiding presentations, I'm dodging the very people paying me, all because of this. 

So when you ask me to consider that it's not real... it's like asking me to consider that the sky is green. I just can't. I spend hours, literally hours, analyzing photos on my phone, zooming in on my jaw, comparing the left side to the right side, looking at the way the skin pulls. If it didn't exist, there wouldn't be a shadow there. If it didn't exist, my mouth wouldn't pull down on that side when I try to smile. I just... I don't know how to make you understand that this is a physical reality, and it is completely destroying my life. How could I possibly invent something that is costing me my livelihood?
Has your concern about your jawline affected your relationships with family or friends?

Yes. Oh, yes, absolutely. It’s... well, it’s honestly ruining everything. You asked about family and friends, and... well, our family gatherings have just started to completely fall apart around this. I used to be the one who hosted everything. Birthdays, holidays, Sunday dinners with my husband’s siblings and all the nieces and nephews. I loved it. But lately? I just can't do it. I can't sit at the dining table with the overhead chandelier casting those harsh downward shadows right onto my jaw. I can't bear the thought of everyone staring at me across the table, seeing how lopsided and heavy my face has gotten. So I make excuses. I say I’m too busy with work, or I’m not feeling well, and we just... we don't see anyone anymore. My husband is so frustrated, and my friends have stopped calling as much because I say no to every lunch or coffee date. 

But the terrible irony is that I'm not actually busy with work, because everything there is collapsing, too. I know I told you about hiding in my car during that one pitch last week, but it’s becoming a pattern. I’ve been cancelling major client presentations at the last minute constantly. I just panic. I get ready, I look in the mirror, and I see that awful sagging skin, and I just completely shut down. Because of all this, my project deadlines are starting to fall apart. I have junior staff waiting on me for approvals, contractors calling me for revisions, and I’m just... I’m sitting in my home office with the blinds drawn, analyzing photos of my jawline instead of doing my job. 

It’s even destroying the good things. My firm was recently nominated for a regional design award—which is a massive milestone, something I’ve worked decades to achieve—and I have been missing all the award-related networking events. There was a huge gala just a few weeks ago. I bought a dress, I had my hair done, but the moment I caught sight of my jaw in the hallway mirror, I just took the dress off and got into bed. I couldn't go. I can’t face being seen by all those successful, polished people. I know they would just look at my face and wonder what happened to me. So, yes, it’s affecting my family, my friends... it’s taking over absolutely everything, Doctor. I'm watching my entire life slip away, and I just don't know how to stop it.
Do you think there's any possibility, no matter how small, that your perception of your jawline might be different from reality?

Doctor, we just keep coming back to this, and I know I sound like a broken record. I really do. But I feel like you're searching for some tiny window of doubt in me, and I just... I don't have it to give you. Like I've been trying to explain, the whole reason I'm here, sitting in this office with you today, is because I absolutely cannot stop seeing this droop and the unevenness around my mouth and my jaw. It is a constant. It's in every single photo, it's in every reflection, every pane of glass I happen to glance at. 

And I know I've already mentioned that people tell me I look fine. My husband says it, my friends say it, and I know you want me to use that as proof that maybe my perception is off. But you have to understand... even when they say those things, what I am seeing with my own two eyes feels so glaringly, undeniably obvious. It is so real to me that it has completely derailed my life. 

I mean, I wouldn't be avoiding my clients if this were just some tiny, passing insecurity! I wouldn't be handing off massive presentations that I spent months preparing for. Do you really think I would sabotage my own architectural firm, hide in my car, and dodge the very people paying me if I thought there was even a small possibility that this flaw wasn't real? 

I wish there was a possibility. God, I wish I could just wake up tomorrow and realize it was all a bad dream and my face was perfectly symmetrical and tight. But when I look in the mirror, the sagging skin is right there. It's dictating every choice I make, every meeting I cancel, every person I avoid. So, no... I don't see how my perception could be different from reality when it is so actively destroying mine.
Have you ever consulted a dermatologist or a plastic surgeon about the appearance of your jawline?

A plastic surgeon? Or a dermatologist? No... no, I haven't actually gone to see one. I mean, I haven't had a consultation or anything like that. I have thought about it, of course. I spend so much time thinking about it. I actually have a whole folder on my computer, right there on my desktop next to my project files, just filled with bookmarks for every prominent facial surgeon in the state. I spend hours looking through their websites, analyzing their before-and-after galleries, trying to find someone, anyone, who had this same awful, heavy droop on the side of their mouth to see if it can even be fixed. 

But to actually call their office? To set up an appointment and go in? I just... I completely freeze. Because if I go, I have to sit in one of those examination rooms. And I know lighting, Doctor, I design commercial spaces for a living. I know exactly how harsh and unforgiving clinical lighting is. It is bright, it is overhead, and it creates the most intense, deep shadows. The thought of sitting in a chair under that glaring light, having a specialist lean in and scrutinize the asymmetry of my jaw, analyzing every sagging millimeter of my skin... it makes my heart pound just talking about it. 

I can barely handle my own reflection in a dim room right now. If I had to sit there while they took those clinical photographs they always take, from every angle... I think I would completely break down. And what if they tell me it is too severe to fix? Or what if they just stare at the unevenness and judge me? I am already hiding from my clients and my own family because I am so ashamed of how I look. The idea of voluntarily walking into a brightly lit room to have a professional dissect this flaw... it is just too terrifying. So, no, I haven't gone. I just sit at home, staring at their websites, too paralyzed to actually do anything about it.
Have you ever received any kind of medical evaluation or consultation regarding the appearance of your jawline?

Well, like I was just saying a minute ago about the plastic surgeons... no. No medical evaluations at all. Not for the jawline, and honestly, not for anything else either lately. I haven't even been to my primary care doctor for my regular annual physical in over a year and a half. 

I used to go every single fall, just for the standard blood pressure check and all that, but... well, it's the exact same problem I just mentioned with the surgeons. Those standard medical exam rooms. You go in, you sit on that awful crinkly paper on the examination table, and you're just trapped under those fluorescent panels in the ceiling. Doctors are trained to observe things, right? That is their entire job, to look for abnormalities. And I just know—I know it in my bones—that if I sit there, even if I'm just there for a sinus infection or a routine check-up, they are going to look at my face and see how the skin on my jaw just hangs there. They'll see the unevenness. 

What if they ask me about it? What if they think I've had a stroke or some kind of nerve damage because it looks so lopsided and heavy, and they bring it up out of nowhere? Like, 'Oh, have you noticed this severe sagging on the lower half of your face?' I would absolutely die. I would just die of humiliation right there on the spot. I can't bear the thought of a doctor scrutinizing it, or writing it down in my medical chart as some kind of visible deformity. So, no. No consultations, no evaluations. I just avoid all medical offices entirely now. It's the only way I can protect myself from being put under a microscope like that.
Has your concern about your jawline led to any significant changes in your daily routine or activities?

Oh, God, yes. Yes, it has. I mean, I... I touched on this a bit before, about dodging my clients, but it's... it's so much worse than just that. It's infiltrated absolutely everything. My entire routine is just... gone. It's completely dictated by this... this awful sagging on my face. 

Just last week, for example, I had this massive client presentation. It was for a commercial complex we've been designing for over eight months. I was the lead architect. I had the blueprints finalized, the 3D renderings were perfect, I knew every square inch of that project backward and forward. And the morning of the presentation, I got up, I started getting ready, and I looked in the mirror, and... the droop on my jawline, the way the skin just hung there, so heavy and uneven... it was all I could see. I spent two hours trying different makeup techniques, contouring, trying to create shadows to hide it, but nothing worked. It just looked worse. And I realized I couldn't go in there. I couldn't stand at the front of a conference room, with all those executives staring at me, scrutinizing my face while I tried to talk about building aesthetics. So... I cancelled. At the very last minute. I called my junior partner, told him he had to do it, and I stayed in my house with the blinds drawn. 

And it's not just that one presentation. My project deadlines are slipping because I can't bring myself to go to site visits or meet with contractors. I just sit at my desk at home, agonizing over how I look, instead of working. And there was this awards banquet a few weeks ago... my firm was nominated for a regional design award. It's a huge networking event, the kind of thing you have to go to if you want to keep bringing in high-profile work. I bought a dress and everything. But when the night came, I just... I couldn't face being seen. I couldn't bear the thought of all those people, my peers, looking at my lopsided jaw. So I skipped it. 

And it's bleeding into my personal life, too. Family gatherings... I used to love them. But now, if my sister invites us over for a barbecue, or if there's a birthday dinner, I find an excuse. I say I'm working late, or I have a migraine. My husband is getting so frustrated, and I don't blame him, but I just... I can't let people see me like this. Everything is just falling apart around this one thing, and I don't know how to stop it.
Do you think about your jawline during most of your waking hours?

Most of my waking hours? Honestly, Doctor, it feels like all of my waking hours. It is... it is a constant, unending loop in my head. From the absolute second I open my eyes in the morning, before my feet even hit the floor, I am already dreading having to go into the bathroom and look in the mirror. 

I mean, that is exactly why I am sitting in this chair talking to you today. I am here because I just cannot stop seeing it. No matter what I do, I cannot stop seeing this awful, heavy droop and the unevenness around my mouth and my jaw. Every single time I pass a reflection—whether it's the bathroom mirror, or a dark window in the kitchen, or even just catching my face in the blank screen of my iPad—it's right there. And photos? I can't even look at photos anymore. If someone pulls out a camera, I panic, because I know exactly how lopsided and deformed I’m going to look in the picture. 

And the worst part is, my husband, or my sister, they try to tell me I'm crazy. They'll say, 'Oh, you look fine,' or 'I don't even see what you're talking about, it's just normal aging.' But it doesn't help. Even when people tell me I look perfectly fine, it feels so incredibly obvious to me. It is glaring. It feels like a neon sign flashing on the lower half of my face, broadcasting this huge flaw to the entire world. How could they not see it? It's all I see! 

And because it feels so obvious, and because it is literally all I can think about from the moment I wake up until the moment I finally manage to fall asleep, that is why I've started avoiding my presentations and dodging my clients like I was telling you about. I just can't function. I can't stand at the front of a room and talk about spatial design when my brain is just screaming at me about how my jaw is sagging. It takes up absolutely every ounce of my mental energy. So, yes... yes, I think about it constantly. I don't really think about much else anymore.
Do you feel like your concerns about your jawline are interfering with your ability to enjoy social activities or maintain relationships?

Well, yes, absolutely. I mean, I know I was just talking about this a little bit ago, but it really does bleed into absolutely everything. Like I said before, I cancelled that major client presentation at the very last minute, and I've been completely missing out on all that award-related networking... and it all boils down to the fact that I just cannot face being seen. I simply can't do it. 

And as for my personal relationships... yes. It's devastating. I know I mentioned earlier that my project deadlines and my family gatherings have started to fall apart around this, but it's... it's just so hard on the people around me, and that makes it even harder on me. My husband, for instance. I bring him up because he used to be my biggest supporter, and now I can just see the exhaustion in his eyes. When my sister invites us to those barbecues or birthday dinners that I used to love, and I make up yet another excuse about a migraine or having to work late... he knows. He knows I'm not really working. He knows I'm just hiding in the house because of my face. 

We used to be so social, you know? We used to love going to events or out to dinner, and now I can't even sit across a table from my own family without obsessing over whether the room's lighting is casting a shadow on the droop in my jaw. I can't enjoy a single conversation because the whole time someone is talking to me, I'm just thinking, 'They're looking at it. They see how lopsided I am.' 

So, I just isolate myself. I stay home. I let the networking events pass by, I let the family dinners happen without me, and I just watch my whole life sort of... shrink. It's like I'm choosing this awful sagging skin over my own family and my career, which sounds insane, I know it does, but the panic of being looked at is just too overwhelming. So, yes, to answer your question, it is interfering with every single relationship and social activity I have. I don't really even have a social life anymore.
Do you think it's possible that your jawline actually looks normal to others, but you're just perceiving it differently?

I mean... I don't know. I really don't know. When you say "normal," it's just... it's hard for me to even process that word in relation to my face right now. Because, like I was saying before, my husband and my sister, they try to tell me that. They say, "You look fine, it's just normal aging, nobody sees what you see." And part of me, maybe a tiny, logical part of my brain that's still functioning, wants to believe them. I want to believe that I'm just... blowing this out of proportion, that I'm seeing a monster in the mirror that isn't really there. 

But then I look in the mirror, Doctor, and it is just so real. It is so physically present. I can see the exact angle where the skin sags, I can see the exact difference in millimeters between the left side and the right side. I see the shadows it casts. And it's not just a fleeting thought, it's a visual reality to me. So when people tell me it looks normal, I just... I feel like they're lying to me. Or they're just trying to be nice, you know? Like when you tell someone they look great when they're sick, just to make them feel better. 

I try to tell myself, "Okay, maybe it's the lighting in this bathroom, maybe it's just the angle of this photograph." But then I'll spend an hour analyzing a picture, zooming in on my jaw, comparing it to pictures of myself from five years ago, ten years ago. And the evidence is right there! The droop is right there! So how can it be that I'm just perceiving it differently? How can something that feels so massive, so glaringly obvious to me, be invisible to everyone else? 

It makes me feel like I'm losing my mind. Truly. Because if they really don't see it, then what is wrong with my eyes? What is wrong with my brain? But then I go right back to the mirror, and there it is again. The sagging. The unevenness. It's like this vicious cycle. I want to believe it's just my perception, I really do, because that would mean I don't actually look as awful as I feel... but I just can't reconcile what they're saying with what I am physically seeing with my own two eyes every single day. So, I don't know. I just don't know what's real anymore.
Is your concern about your jawline focused on a specific feature, such as its shape, size, or symmetry?

Well, yes, it’s... I know I keep coming back to this, and I apologize if I’m talking in circles, but it really comes down to the symmetry. Or, I guess, the complete lack of it. It’s the unevenness. Like I was trying to explain earlier, I am here in this chair specifically because I cannot stop obsessing over this heavy droop around my mouth and my jaw. It’s the shape of it, the way it sags, but mostly it's how incredibly lopsided it makes my entire face look. 

I look at lines and structures all day for my work, you know, trying to make sure a space has balance and proportion, and then I look at my own face and the balance is just... it's completely ruined. One side pulls down so much more than the other. I literally trace the line of it in my head all day long. And I know I already brought this up, but I really can't stop seeing it in every single photo and every passing reflection. The rearview mirror in my car, for instance, is honestly a nightmare for me because the daylight catches the shadow of that exact uneven droop and highlights exactly how asymmetrical it is. 

So when people tell me I look fine, or that my face is perfectly normal, it just... it baffles me. It frustrates me to tears because the unevenness is so glaringly obvious to me. It’s not just in my head, it’s a physical defect right there on my jawline. It feels so obvious and so humiliating that, like I said before, it’s the entire reason I’ve started completely avoiding my clients and canceling my presentations. How can I stand up in front of a room of people to present a design when my own face is sagging so unevenly? I just... I can't do it. The lopsided shape of it is literally all I can focus on.
Do you worry about any other physical characteristics besides your jawline?

No... no, not really. I mean, maybe years ago I would have worried about my weight or my hair, just normal things women my age think about, but now? Now there is absolutely no room in my brain for anything else. It is entirely, one hundred percent focused on this one area. 

I know I sound like a broken record today, and I appreciate your patience with me, I really do, but I am sitting here in this office because I just cannot stop seeing this droop and the unevenness around my mouth and my jaw. It is completely all-consuming. You ask if I worry about other features, but how could I? I can't look at a single photo of myself without immediately zeroing in on the sagging. Every reflection I walk past—whether it's a glass storefront downtown, or the microwave door in my kitchen, or just the dark screen of my laptop—my eyes dart straight to the lower half of my face. 

And I know we just talked about how my family tells me I look fine, but it really doesn't matter what they say. It doesn't change anything for me because it feels so overwhelmingly obvious. It’s so severe and so humiliating that, like I was saying, I’ve started completely avoiding my presentations at work. I'm dodging my clients. I'm literally throwing away my career as an architect because I cannot bear the thought of them staring at my lopsided mouth while I'm trying to explain a floor plan. So, no, I don't care about my nose or my eyes or my stomach or anything else. It's just this. This one, horrible, uneven droop that I can't escape.
Do you think it's possible that your jawline looks normal to everyone else, but you're the only one who sees a problem with it?

I know you're asking the same question again, just in a different way, and I... I understand why you're asking it. You're trying to get me to see reason, to step outside of my own head. And like I said before, I do hear my husband and my sister when they say I look fine, when they swear up and down that my jawline looks completely normal to them. I hear the words coming out of their mouths. But... I just can't internalize it. I can't believe it. Because how could I be the only one seeing it when it is just so incredibly obvious? 

I mean, I'm here in this office today, sitting across from you, specifically because I cannot stop seeing this droop. I can't stop seeing the unevenness around my mouth and my jaw. It's not just a passing thought, it's a constant, glaring reality every single time I look at a photograph of myself. Every time I catch a glimpse of my reflection in a window, or a mirror, or even just a shiny surface, it's right there. It's so pronounced, so physically undeniable to me, that it honestly doesn't matter if someone else tells me it's normal. 

Because if it's normal, then why do I feel so hideous? Why is it so obvious to me that I've completely changed my life because of it? Like I was telling you earlier, I've started avoiding my presentations at work. I'm actively dodging my clients. I'm an architect, I'm supposed to be leading meetings and standing in front of people explaining complex designs, and instead, I'm hiding in my office because I am so terrified that they're all staring at this sagging, lopsided mess of a jawline. If I'm the only one who sees it, then why does it feel like everyone in the room is judging me for it? I just... I can't accept that it's only in my head when it has completely taken over my reality. So, yes, maybe it's possible that they don't see it the way I do, but to me... to me, it's the only thing that's real.
Do you think it's possible that your perception of your jawline is a delusion?

A delusion? Like... like I'm crazy? I... I know you have to ask these things, and I know I keep repeating myself, but it really is so hard to even entertain that word. Delusion. Because... well, like I keep saying, I'm sitting here in this chair today, talking to you, because I just cannot stop seeing this droop. I can't stop seeing the unevenness around my mouth and my jaw. It is right there. 

If it were a delusion, wouldn't it come and go? Wouldn't it be something I only imagine sometimes? Because this... this is constant. Every single photo I look at, every time I catch my reflection in the bathroom mirror, or the hallway window, or even just the reflection on my phone screen before it lights up... it's there. The sagging, the lopsidedness, it is staring right back at me. And I know, I know I've brought this up a dozen times already, and I know my family says I look fine, but how can it be a delusion when it feels so incredibly, physically obvious to me? 

It’s so real to me that, as I’ve explained, it has completely derailed my life. I mean, I’ve started actively avoiding my clients. I'm canceling my presentations at the firm. I’m an architect with over thirty years of experience, and I am hiding in my office because I am so deeply ashamed of how my face looks. If it were just a delusion, just some trick of my mind, would I really be throwing away my entire career over it? Would I really be too terrified to stand up in front of a room and point to a blueprint because I'm convinced everyone is staring at my jawline? It just... it feels too real, too heavy, too devastating to just be a delusion. It's my face. It's right there.
Do you think it's possible that the droop and unevenness you see in your jawline is something that only you can see and not actually there?
